phonics.stretchNote: Only if the main game was easy. Stop at the first wobble; a stretch that becomes a struggle teaches the wrong lesson. We never go on to next week's sounds early: school's order matters.

maths.topic: Circles and triangles, and where things are
stems: "Is it round, or does it have straight sides?"
"Where is teddy? On, under, next to or in?"
maths.source: From the 13 November school update: circles and triangles, spotting shapes around us, and describing position. Home practice runs a week behind school for maths.
everyday: Meals: a round plate, a sandwich cut into triangles. Which is which?
Out and about: spot a circle (a wheel, a clock) and a triangle (a road sign, a roof).
Tidy up: put the teddy on the bed, the book under the chair, the cup next to the plate.
Maps: school is looking at maps. Draw your street together: a circle for a tree, a triangle for a roof.

steps.do: Find three round things at home: a plate, a coin, a lid.
steps.say: Round all the way. No corners. That's a circle.

steps.do: Trace round a cup on paper to make a circle.
Your child finds one more circle in the room.

questions.say: Which one is round, like a circle?

questions.hint: A corner is where two sides meet. Can you find one on the circle?

questions.say: Which one is not a circle?

challenge.label: Challenge: one more, one less, up to 10
challenge.paper: make a number track on the stairs, 1 to 10. Stand on 6: one step up? one step down?

questions.hint: Six, then count on one.

questions.say: Which number and one more makes 9?
questions.hint: One less than 9: count back one.

questions.say: Four and four more. How many altogether?
questions.hint: A double. Four fingers on each hand.

steps.do: Make a triangle with three straws, spoons or pencils.
steps.say: One, two, three sides. Three corners.

steps.do: Cut a slice of toast into triangles.
Your child makes a triangle for you to count the sides.

questions.say: How many sides does a triangle have?
questions.hint: Count the sides with your finger.

questions.say: How many corners does a triangle have?
questions.hint: Touch each corner as you count.

challenge.label: Challenge: one more, one less, up to 10
challenge.paper: ten raisins in a line. Cover the last one: how many now? Add one back: how many?

questions.hint: Eight, then count on one.

questions.say: Which number and one more makes 7?
questions.hint: One less than 7: count back one.

questions.say: Three and three more. How many altogether?
questions.hint: A double. Three fingers on each hand.

steps.do: Mix up some round things and some triangles (toast, a sign drawn on paper). Sort them into two piles.
Hold one up.
steps.say: Circle or triangle? How do you know?

questions.hint: Count the sides with your finger.

questions.hint: Nine, then count on one: all your fingers.

questions.say: Which number and one more makes 10?
questions.hint: One less than 10: put one finger down.

questions.say: Five and five more. How many altogether?
questions.hint: A double. All your fingers.

steps.do: A teddy and a box. Put teddy on the box, then under it, next to it, in it.
Your child hides teddy and tells you where: on, under, next to or in.
Draw a map of your room or street together: a circle for a rug or a tree, a triangle for a roof.

lastWeek: Phonics: v, w, x, y and the tricky words and, has, his and her.
English: Oliver's Vegetables (Vivian French): remembering the vegetables in the story, writing soup lists with bullet points, and making vegetable soup in class. The children chopped and tasted it.
Maths: circles and triangles: making and comparing them, spotting them around us, and describing where things are.
Understanding the World: Diwali and the story of Rama and Sita, and Remembrance Day (decorating poppies).
